A Michelson setup measures refractive index from fringe changes: evacuating the cell changes the optical path twice, because the beam travels through it going out and back. Convert the counted fringe shift into the corresponding path difference, divide by twice the cell length, then add one to obtain the original index. Keep metres and the laser wavelength in the same units; the result will be only slightly above one for a dilute gas.

eval.content: We are planning a walk around the estuary and someone called the water brackish. I know that means it is between fresh and salt water, but I would like to explain where that usually happens without making it sound too technical. We will be near the river mouth at high tide, and the group includes children who keep asking why the water does not taste the same everywhere.

That is a good place to explain it. An estuary is where river water and seawater meet, so tides can push salty water upstream while the river carries fresh water down. The mixture changes from place to place and hour to hour, which is why animals there have to cope with shifting salt levels. You can point out the visible clues too: mudflats, reeds, changing currents, and birds feeding where the two waters mix. Calling it a blend rather than a separate kind of water usually lands well with children.
Where is water most likely to be brackish, and what is a simple way to describe it to our group?

eval.content: My nephew found a nature video where tiny wasps lay eggs in caterpillars, and he was upset because the caterpillar is alive while the larvae grow. I told him nature does not always fit the friendly examples in his book, but I want to explain the relationship accurately without being graphic. The video says the larvae use the caterpillar for food and later emerge from it. We are trying to label the relationship for his food-web page.

You can say that the wasp benefits while the caterpillar is harmed, which is the core pattern he needs. The more specific term matters because the young develop in or on one host and eventually kill it, unlike a typical parasite that often feeds without immediately killing the host. It is fine to acknowledge that it feels harsh; ecosystems contain many interactions that are uncomfortable to watch, and the point of the label is to describe what happens, not to approve of it.
What is the best name for that wasp-and-caterpillar relationship, where the larvae grow inside the living host?

eval.content: I am sorting photos from a family trip through the mountains and want to identify the landforms we saw.

Glaciers reshape landscapes by scraping rock, carrying sediment, and leaving distinctive deposits as they retreat. Look for broad valleys, ridges of debris, polished surfaces, and isolated boulders that do not match the local rock. The shape of a feature tells you whether ice carved it, deposited it, or merely passed nearby, so a photograph with scale and surrounding terrain is especially useful. A map can help too, because former ice paths often line up with whole valleys rather than one spot.
